Therefore we have seen the Messenger of God ﷺ, who is the model for the community of faith, supplicating his Lord and saying: "O God, I seek Your forgiveness for every deed by which I intended Your Face but in which there mixed with me what is not for You" (2).

The deed of faith is that which is purely for God, and according to the sincerity is the reward. Among people is one who does righteousness which agrees with something in himself, such as that it helps him in orderly living or in saving expenses or otherwise, so he continues in it, not for God but for his own interest.

Concerning these, God the Exalted says: ﴿And among the people is one who worships God on an edge; if good befalls him, he is reassured by it, but if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face. He has lost the world and the Hereafter. That is the manifest loss﴾ [22:11]

And like the merchant who adheres to truthfulness in his trade, not out of love for truthfulness itself, but out of desire for reputation and renown and gaining more customers. Such people obtain from the world according to their striving for it, and God does not deprive them of the fruit of their efforts, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter, We increase for him in his tilth; and whoever desires the tilth of this world, We give him of it, but he has no share in the Hereafter﴾ [42:20]

So their intentions in deeds are like a caravan heading in one direction, yet each has a goal he strives for: this one strives for food or a delicious meal, this one strives for a beautiful woman, this one strives for a lesson of knowledge from which he benefits, and another strives to see the one he loves. The poet expressed this meaning in his saying:

I set out with the caravan toward the one I desire, and I said to them: "Go on, eat and take what is your share in it."
But let me meet the one I hope for—my eye sees Him, and my conscience converses with Him.

Likewise, the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, wants His servant to seek Him for His own sake, not out of fear of His Fire, nor out of desire for His Paradise. There is a difference between being blessed by God's favor and being blessed by looking at God. You in Paradise eat, not from hunger nor from need, but merely for enjoyment.

Therefore, He, glorified is He, says of the martyrs: ﴿And do not think of those who have been killed in the way of God as dead; rather, they are alive with their Lord, being provided for﴾ [3:169]. This "with-ness" suffices them, and that they look to God, glorified and exalted is He.

Therefore Rābi'a al-'Adawiyya said: "O God, if You know that I worship You out of desire for Your Paradise, then deprive me of it; and if You know that I worship You out of fear of Your Fire, then cast me into it. But I worship You because You are worthy to be worshipped."

There is no doubt that few people sincerely purify their intention for God, and that most perform deeds with whatever intention happens, which this matter does not benefit them nor do they concern themselves with it, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And most of them do not believe in God except that they are associating [others with Him]﴾ [12:106]

They divided their religion like caravans whose directions and intentions differ, ﴿and became sects...﴾ (Ar-Rum). *Shi'ah* (a party or faction) is the plural *shi'ah*, meaning a group that cooperates on some matter, whether good or evil. Good, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, among his partisans was Abraham﴾ (As-Saffat).

Or evil, as in: ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land and made its people into factions...﴾ (Al-Qasas).

In another verse: ﴿Say, He is able to send upon you a punishment from above you or from beneath your feet, or to confound you into factions and make you taste the violence of one another...﴾ (Al-An'am).

And His saying: ﴿Each faction, with what they have, is pleased﴾ (Ar-Rum). This is because of the temporal authority they hold and the standing they have, fearing that it would be shaken, like the temporal authority that prevented the Jews of Medina from believing in the Messenger of God, although they knew him as they know their own sons, and knew his time. They used to dwell in Medina awaiting his appearance, and all of that was in their Torah, to the extent that they would say: "He will appear at the end of time; we will follow him, and kill you with him, a killing like that of 'Ad and Iram" (1).

﴿So when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it...﴾ (Al-Baqarah).

Why? To preserve their temporal authority. They were people of knowledge, wealth and standing. When Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent, he abolished this authority, for there is no word after his word (ﷺ). As for those among them who remained firm upon their true religion and acted by what is in the Torah, they believed in Muhammad, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and other rabbis of the Jews.

Temporal authority is what stands between people and the truth they believe in. This temporal authority is what we see today in these factions and parties, each of which claims that it is upon the truth and that everything else is falsehood.

He, Exalted, says: ﴿If the truth had followed their desires, the heavens and the earth would have been corrupted, and whoever is in them...﴾ (Al-Mu'minun).

Thus each of them butts against the others to exalt his own doctrine and to appear on the scene.

1. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said, from Asim ibn Amr, from Qatadah al-Ansari, from some of their shaykhs, who said: "By God, it was about us and about them, meaning the Ansar and the Jews who were their neighbours, that this story was revealed: ﴿And when there came to them a Book from God confirming what was with them, and previously they had been seeking victory over those who disbelieved; but when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it...﴾ (Al-Baqarah). They said: 'We had dominated them by force for ages in the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance), and we were people of polytheism while they were people of the Book. They used to say: a prophet is about to be sent, and we will follow him; his time has drawn near. We will kill you with him, a killing like that of 'Ad and Iram. Then when God sent His Messenger from Quraysh and we followed him, they disbelieved in him.'" Cited by Ibn Kathir in his tafsir (1/124).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 30, verse 33:

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, makes clear to us that those who disbelieve in God, or rebel against the method of God, remain in this way captives of this worldly authority. When a shock or a calamity befalls them, which their means cannot repel, they find no refuge but God. So He, glory be to Him, said:

﴿When harm touches people, they call upon their Lord, turning to Him in repentance. Then when He lets them taste mercy from Him, behold, a group of them associate others with their Lord.﴾ (33)

Ḍurr (harm) is that thing from which we suffer and which the soul does not find pleasant. So if harm befalls them and their means do not suffice for deliverance from it, ﴿they call upon their Lord, turning to Him...﴾ (Surah al-Rum), meaning: they return to Him, glory be to Him. Now they know that they have a Lord to whom they resort. This reminds us of what the Arabs said when revelation was delayed from the Messenger of God, and it pleased them, and they said: "The Lord of Muhammad has forsaken him" (1). Glory be to God, now you know that Muhammad has a Lord.

We have said that in the hour of distress and trial, a person does not deceive himself or fool his soul. We have previously mentioned the story of the barber-surgeon who used to take the place of the physician. When medical colleges were established and graduated doctors, one of them went to the village of the barber, and the barber began to attack him, claiming that he was a novice with no experience. But when his son fell ill and he sensed danger, he took him secretly in the darkness of night and went with him to the doctor. Why? Because he would not deceive himself at that moment.

﴿Then when He lets them taste mercy from Him, behold, a group of them associate others with their Lord.﴾ (33) Meaning: they return to what they were upon of associating others with God.

When we reflect on this matter, we find that the Qur'an presented it once in the singular form, saying: ﴿And when harm touches man, he calls upon his Lord, turning to Him in repentance...﴾ (8) (Surah al-Zumar).

And He said: ﴿And when harm touches man, he calls upon Us, lying on his side, or sitting, or standing. But when We remove his harm from him, he passes on as if he had never called upon Us regarding a harm that touched him...﴾ (12) (Surah Yunus).

But speaking of the individual person is not sufficient to establish the phenomenon, because a single person may humble himself before his Lord and return to Him after having dared to disobey Him, and that happens between him and himself, so he does not expose himself before people. Therefore God wished to establish this matter among all people, so that they might expose one another. So He mentioned here: ﴿And when harm touches people, they call upon their Lord, turning to Him...﴾ (33) (Surah al-Rum).

And in another verse: ﴿And when they board the ship, they call upon God, sincere to Him in religion. But when He delivers them safely to land, immediately they associate others with Him.﴾ (65) (Surah al-'Ankabut).

Here He used the plural form, exposing the disbelievers before one another. Perhaps among these callers there was someone who used to incite them against God and divert them from faith in Him, and now he is calling and beseeching. When their affair is exposed, that is more conducive to their uprightness and more conducive to ensuring that no one is arrogant toward anyone else.

Therefore we have said, in the balance of prayer, that it makes people equal: the ordinary man sits beside one whom he did not expect to sit beside, and finds him humbled with him, submitting to the Imam... etc. In prayer, all are equal, and all benefit from this equality, taking a lesson from it, so that no one is arrogant toward anyone after it.

We pause here at ﴿mass (touch)...﴾ (33), which is a light touch. The meaning is a slight touch of harm, and yet their means were too narrow to repel it, and they cried out seeking help.

And the word ﴿adhaqahum (He let them taste)...﴾ (33): dhawq (tasting) is one of the senses of man, by which he perceives food as it passes over a specific area of the tongue. When food passes beyond this area, a person does not feel its taste.

So the pleasure of food is confined to this area of the mouth, and tasting is the strongest of the soul's responses in receiving flavor; therefore they say in proverbs: "What passes the tongue becomes foul" (al-lī yafūt fī al-lisān biqā natān).

And consider how the Truth, glory be to Him, used idhāqa (making to taste) in the domain of punishment when He struck for us this parable: ﴿And God presents an example: a city that was secure and tranquil, its provision coming to it abundantly from every place, but it denied the favors of God, so God made it taste the garment of hunger and fear for what they used to do.﴾ (112) (Surah al-Nahl).

He mentioned tasting even though clothing encompasses the whole body, and likewise hunger and fear, each of which is a sensation that takes hold of the whole person. Yet He said ﴿He made it taste...﴾ (112) because tasting is the strongest kind of perception.

And the word ﴿minhu (from Him)...﴾ (33): meaning from God, Exalted, that is, without means; or ﴿adhaqahum minhu...﴾ (33): meaning in place of harm, mercy, and He delivered them from harm with mercy. Just as tasting, although it indicates the intense response of the one receiving, also indicates light handling with gentleness, as you say: "I tasted the food," or you say: "By God, I did not taste food at so-and-so's," meaning: I did not eat there, a fortiori.

Therefore the Truth, glory be to Him, expressed mercy here by tasting, because the mercy of this world does not encompass all the mercy of God; its little is in this world, and most of it is in the Hereafter.

We note in His saying, Exalted: ﴿...behold, a group of them associate others with their Lord﴾ (33), whereas in the other verse: ﴿...behold, they associate others﴾ (65), why did He say in the first ﴿a group of them﴾ (33) and in the other ﴿they﴾ (65), without excepting any of them?

They said: because the first verse speaks of those who called upon God on land, and people on land are usually different, among them the righteous and the wicked, the obedient and the disobedient; they differ in their reaction. So the believers, when they witnessed deliverance and the mercy of God, said: "Praise be to God who saved us," whereas the polytheists returned to their disbelief and obstinacy.

As for the other verse, it speaks of those who called upon God at sea, and those who board the sea are usually of one type. They do not board it as a means of travel but for luxury, as we see some take for themselves a yacht, for example, or a floating platform where they gather their followers and those of their kind, and they surely gather around something they love. They are of one creed, one way, and one conduct.

So since these were at sea, they must have been hardened criminals, equal in polytheism and in abandoning God as soon as they felt safe from danger. Therefore the expression here is ﴿idhā (behold)...﴾ (33), the sudden particle, and it is used in another verse, ﴿behold, they associate others﴾ (65), for after God delivered them, they hastened back to what they had been upon of associating others.

In this verse, the Truth, glory be to Him, makes clear to us the reality of man and the extent of his eagerness to bring good to himself. If the good that God has prepared for him makes him insolent and tyrannical, as He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Nay, indeed man transgresses, when he sees himself self-sufficient.﴾ (6-7) (Surah al-'Alaq)

Then he has no escape from returning to his Lord when God shakes off from him all means of good, and threatens him in his soul and in his self, which has not benefited from the signs of God in the cosmos, so that it remains in the custody of God, and He brings upon him the harm that shakes off from him all causes of insolence, arrogance, and self-exaltation.

But he does not surrender himself to the harm that destroys him; rather then he becomes aware that he has a Lord to whom he resorts, and finds no refuge in the cosmos except Him, because he knows well that those whom he took besides God and believed in and disbelieved in God will not benefit him in anything, since he worshipped, apart from God, gods that neither harm nor benefit.

Therefore He, exalted, says: ﴿And when harm touches you at sea, those you call upon vanish, except Him...﴾ (67) (Surah al-Isra). Those whom you call upon do not know your way, and if they knew it, they could not reach you; but as for Me, I am your Lord, the Best Knower of you, able to rescue you and to send down mercy upon you.

So these polytheists associated others with God in time of ease, but in time of hardship and distress none of them deceives himself or fools his soul. He will not say: "Hubal!" Because he knows that Hubal does not hear him or answer him, so it does not benefit him now, and nothing saves him except the true God, for necessity has compelled him to acknowledge Him and call upon Him.

(1) Ibn Kathir mentioned in his tafsir (4/522) from the narration of Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna from al-Aswad ibn Qays, who heard Jundab say: Gabriel was delayed from the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, so the polytheists said: "Muhammad's Lord has forsaken him," and God revealed: ﴿By the morning brightness, and by the night when it is still, your Lord has not forsaken you, nor has He detested you﴾ (Surah al-Duha, 1-3)..
(2) Raghad al-'aysh: it became spacious and pleasant. His saying: ﴿And eat freely therefrom, wherever you wish...﴾ (35) (Surah al-Baqarah), meaning: eat good food, abundantly provided for you therein. (al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/269)..

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 30, verse 34:

Then the Almighty says:

﴿So that they may disbelieve in what We have given them. So enjoy yourselves, for you will soon know.﴾

It may come to mind that the lam in ﴿so that they may disbelieve...﴾ (al-Rum) is the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil), or the lam of causality whose following clause is the cause of what precedes it, as when you say: "Study so that you may succeed." Likewise in the conditional and its response: "If you study, you will succeed," the cause of studying is success.

Does the meaning stand on this understanding? And did God rescue them and let them taste mercy in order that they might disbelieve in Him?

We say: the condition is not the cause of the response's occurrence, as the superficial thinkers of the language understand it. Rather, the response is the cause of the condition, but they did not distinguish between a motivating cause (sabab dafi') and an actual cause (sabab waqi'). The student studies because the successful outcome has come to his mind, and its good effects have appeared to him first, and so they moved him to study.

Thus: the response is a cause of the condition, that is, a motivating cause that impels toward it. So if you want it to occur in reality, put the condition first so that the response comes about.

As you say: "I boarded the car in order to go to Alexandria." Boarding the car is not the cause of your going to Alexandria; rather you first wished to go, so you boarded the car, and when you boarded it, you actually arrived. Thus we say: the condition is a cause of the response as a motivating impulse that drives toward it, and the response is a cause of the condition as an actual reality.

Here, God rescued them from distress and let them taste His mercy, not in order that they disbelieve in Him, but to make clear to them that they have no refuge except in Him, so that they would cling to Him, the Glorified; so the disbeliever among them would believe, and the believer among them would increase in faith. But their reaction came out contrary to that: they disbelieved in God. Therefore they call this lam the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), meaning that their disbelief was the consequence of rescue and mercy.

An example of this—and to God belongs the highest likeness—is that if you took a poor child into your care and raised him in the best upbringing, and when he grew up and matured he disowned you and transgressed against you, you would say to people: "I raised him so that he would transgress against me." The meaning is: I raised him so that he would respect and love me, but the result and the consequence came out otherwise. This indicates the corruption of judgment in the one who raised him, and the baseness and corrupt nature of the one who was raised.

So the expression here, ﴿so that they may disbelieve...﴾ (al-Rum), carries the sense of reproach, because what follows the lam of consequence is not the true cause of what precedes it. The true cause of what precedes it is the counterpart of what follows the lam: He made them taste mercy and rescued them so that they would believe, or so that they would increase in faith, but what came from them was only that they disbelieved.

There are many parallels to this matter in the Qur'an, such as His saying, concerning the story of Moses: ﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up, so that he might become an enemy and a source of grief for them...﴾ (al-Qasas, 8).

It is known that they picked him up so that he would be a delight for their eyes. Had they known this consequence, they would have drowned him or killed him, as they killed other children of the Children of Israel. And as they say in proverbs: "Raise the one who will strangle you" (bi-yirabbi khannaqah).

This is evidence of the heedlessness of the one who picked him up, and also of his stupidity. How, then, when he is killing boys at this very time, does he not suspect a child who came in a chest cast upon the sea? Is this not an indication that his family wanted to save him from being killed? But as He, the Glorified, said: ﴿And know that God comes between a man and his heart...﴾ (al-Anfal, 24).[1]

You kill children out of a dream that the soothsayers told you about: one will come to your door whom you fear, and you will take him and raise him in your lap, and the loss of your kingdom will be at his hands. So do not think that you can outwit God.

The story shows the failure of Pharaoh and the failure of the soothsayers. If you believed the soothsayers in what they told you, then what is the point of killing children, when you will not know who will be the cause of the loss of your kingdom, and you will not be able to get hold of him? So why take precautions?

Therefore, human thinking must be within the framework that above humans there is a Lord, and the Lord assigns the enemy so that he brings an enemy of his own who will destroy him, and He, the Glorified, is the best of planners. True planning is that it be hidden, so that the one planned against does not perceive it.

And our situation in the twentieth century has reached the point that we say: "Frankness is the cunning of the twentieth century." That is: whoever wants to scheme, let him speak the truth and be frank, because we have become in an age in which frankness and speaking the truth have diminished, to the point that when you tell people the truth, they suspect you and find it unlikely that your words are the truth. Like the one who told a group seeking to kill him: "I will go to such-and-such a place at such-and-such a time," and they said: "He is misleading us and scheming against us," although he was truthful in what he told them.

After Moses, peace be upon him, was raised in Pharaoh's house, and then his Lord charged him with the message, and he went to Pharaoh calling him to God, He said to him: ﴿Did We not raise you among us as a child, and you remained among us for some of your years?﴾ (al-Shu'ara, 18).

Yes, You raised me as a child, but the One who raised me and you is the One who sent me to you. I am dutiful toward the Supreme Nurturer before I am dutiful toward you. In this is an indication that God's care is the origin of the upbringing of whom you love. So beware of saying: "I raised my son until he became such-and-such," but rather take up the means of upbringing, and leave the Supreme Nurturer who truly raises.

This meaning was perceived by the poet, who said:

If you do not find care in your sons, then the hopeful one has lied and the one who hopes has failed.

So Moses, whom Gabriel raised, is an unbeliever, and Moses, whom Pharaoh raised, is a messenger.

Then He, the Glorified, says: ﴿So enjoy yourselves, for you will soon know.﴾ (al-Rum, 34) Because he disbelieved, so as to enjoy his disbelief in this world, since faith has demanding requirements that burden the soul. It commands you to do what is heavy on your self and forbids you what the self loves. As for the idols they worshipped besides God and other deities, they have no requirements and no method.

But it is the enjoyment of worldly life, and the enjoyment of this world is little, because the world, as far as you are concerned, is the duration of your stay in it. Do not say that it extends from Adam to the Hour, for this long life does not concern you at all. What concerns you is your own life.

Whatever the lifespan of a person in this world, it is short, and his enjoyment of it is little. Moreover, this short life is presumed rather than certain, for death may overtake you at any moment, and whoever dies, his resurrection has come.[2]

Therefore the Real, the Glorified and Exalted, left death undefined and scattered its times among creation: one dies before being born, another dies as a child, another dies as a youth... and so on. The indefiniteness of death as to cause, time and place is itself clear explanation, for it becomes a figure before each of us, awaiting us at any moment, so that one prepares for it.

We note here that the Qur'anic style conjoined the imperative ﴿So enjoy yourselves...﴾ (al-Rum, 34) to the imperfect verb ﴿so that they may disbelieve...﴾ (al-Rum, 34), while in another place He, the Glorified, said: ﴿So that they may disbelieve in what We have given them, and so that they may enjoy themselves...﴾ (al-'Ankabut, 66). Thus He made the enjoying not subject to the imperative verb, but to the causal particle: "so that they may disbelieve and so that they may enjoy themselves."

Therefore they differed about this lam: is it the lam of command or the lam of causation? ﴿For you will soon know﴾ (al-Rum, 34) came after ﴿So enjoy yourselves...﴾ (al-Rum, 34), and this one came conjoined to ﴿so that they may disbelieve...﴾ (al-'Ankabut, 66). So it is as if He said: "Disbelieve and enjoy yourselves, but you will know the consequence of that."

For this reason, those who say the lam here is the lam of causation say it is kasra-vowelled (kasra), whereas the lam of command is sukun-vowelled (sakin). When they saw the lam vowelled with kasra, they said it was the lam of causation. But whoever understood the meaning among them said: since the context conjoins the imperative "enjoy yourselves" to the imperfect verb linked to the lam, the lam is also a lam of command, since the imperative verb is conjoined to it, and here it is for threat.

But why is it vowelled with kasra when the rule is that it is sakin? One grammarian said: the lam of command is sukun-vowelled, but it may be vowelled with kasra, and he cited this verse: ﴿so that they may disbelieve in what We have given them, and so that they may enjoy themselves...﴾ (al-'Ankabut, 66).

To those who say it is the lam of causation, we say: if you hear the lam of causation, know that it means the lam of consequence, since disbelief and enjoyment were not the cause of the tasting of mercy.

And to you who say it is the lam of command, they will say to you: why is it vowelled with kasra? In the Qur'an there are many instances showing that it may be vowelled with kasra. Read His saying: ﴿And proclaim among the people the pilgrimage; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every deep mountain pass. That they may witness benefits for themselves...﴾ (al-Hajj, 27-28). Here the lam is vowelled with kasra because it is the lam of causation.

Then He said after it: ﴿Then let them end their unkemptness and fulfil their vows and circumambulate the Ancient House﴾ (al-Hajj, 29). Here the lam is sukun-vowelled because it is the lam of command.

In another verse both lams are combined: ﴿Let the one of wealth spend from his wealth...﴾ (al-Talaq, 7). Here the lam of command is kasra-vowelled because it stands at the beginning of the sentence, and in the language one does not begin with a sukun, so it is vowelled with kasra to avoid the sukun. Then He, the Glorified, said: ﴿And whoever has his provision restricted, let him spend from what God has given him...﴾ (al-Talaq, 7). Here the lam of command is sukun-vowelled because it stands in the middle of the speech.

Therefore the writers of the Mushaf must heed this matter, and know that the Word of God prevails. The writers of the Mushaf's script overlooked that it is built, from its beginning to its end, on continuity (wasl), even at the end of the surah al-Nas and the beginning of al-Fatiha: we say ﴿Who whispers in the breasts of people, of jinn and of people. In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate...﴾.

So the end of the Qur'an is joined to its beginning, so that it never ends. Accordingly, do not write ﴿Let the one of wealth spend from his wealth...﴾ (al-Talaq, 7) with kasra; rather with sukun, because it is joined to what precedes it.

The phrase ﴿For you will soon know﴾ (al-Rum, 34) indicates deferment and encompasses the whole future, whether near or distant. So it is a precaution for one who will die right after the address, or who will die a long time after it.

1. That is, God controls the human heart and changes its intention as He wills; a person does not own his heart, but God is the One who owns it. (al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/179).
2. Al-Daylami narrated it in his Musnad (1117) from Anas, raised: "When one of you dies, his resurrection has come." Al-'Ajluni said in Kashf al-Khafa' (2618): "It is related from Anas: Remember death often, for if you remember it in wealth it will sour it for you, and if you remember it in hardship it will widen it for you. Death is the resurrection; when one of you dies, his resurrection has come; he sees what good and evil he has."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 30, verse 35:

Then the Truthful One, glorified is He, says:

﴿Or have We sent down to them an authority, so that it speaks of what they have been associating with Him?﴾

The word *am* (أم, "or") does not come at the beginning, because it is a particle that expresses choice between two matters, as you say: "Did Zayd come, or 'Amr?" It must therefore come between two opposites. The implied meaning is: "Have they followed their desires, or do they have a Book sent down to them, which would be a proof for them in their polytheism?" Since no Book was sent down to them that would be a proof for them, nothing remains but the other option, that they followed their desires.

As for the verb ﴿We sent down...﴾ (ar-Rum), sending down (inzal) implies the elevation of the one from whom it is sent down, and that the one upon whom it is sent down is lower. So sending down is from the height of lordship to the humility of servanthood. We have not seen the sending down; rather, the one who first received the Qur'an and directly experienced the revelation is the one who saw it and informed us of it.

The original sense of sending down is that it comes from God, exalted is He. When God sends down something to us, it is only so that He, glorified is He, may give us a share of this height, whether the height is immaterial, because God, glorified is He, has no place, or a tangible height, as in ﴿And We sent down iron, wherein is mighty power and benefits for mankind...﴾ (al-Hadid, 25).

Sultan (سلطان, "authority") derives from *tasallut* (domination), and it indicates strength, whether the strength of argument and proof, so that whoever persuades you with argument and proof has power over you, or the strength of compulsion and coercion, like one who forces you to do something while you are unwilling. As for the authority of argument, you act while you are content and convinced.

When we survey the word sultan, we find that God Most High presents it to us in the situation of Iblis in the Hereafter, when he disowns those who followed him: ﴿And I had over you no authority except that I invited you, and you responded to me. So do not blame me but blame yourselves...﴾ (Ibrahim, 22).

That is: I had no authority of argument and persuasion by which I captured your hearts, and I had no authority of compulsion by which I subdued your bodies. The reality is that you were (on a hasty course), that as soon as I invited you, you came to me hastening, and you obeyed by choice.

This meaning explains to us something in the Qur'an over which people have debated at length, whether from evil intention or sincere intention: in His saying, once to Iblis, ﴿What prevented you from prostrating...﴾ (Sad, 75), and once more: ﴿What prevented you from not prostrating...﴾ (al-A'raf, 12).

The first indicates the authority of coercion, as if you wanted to prostrate but one who prevented you forcibly from prostrating came; the second indicates the authority of argument and persuasion, so you did not prostrate while you were content and convinced of not prostrating.(1)

As for His saying: ﴿So it speaks of what they have been associating with Him﴾ (ar-Rum, 35), that is: it speaks for what they have been associating with Him. It says: "Do such-and-such," and this came in accordance with their desires.

1. The Imam Abu Yahya Zakariyya al-Ansari said in his book "Fath al-Rahman yakshif ma yaltabis fi al-Qur'an" (p. 137), Dar al-Sabuni edition: "His saying ﴿Unless you prostrate...﴾ (al-A'raf, 12): he said it with the addition of 'la' as in His saying ﴿so that the People of the Book may not know...﴾ (al-Hadid, 29), and in 'Sad' it is without it, which is the original; so its addition here is to emphasize the meaning of negation in 'mana'ak' (prevented you). Or: to imply 'mana'ak' with 'hamalak' (impelled you), and in the second case it is not superfluous in meaning."

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿And when We let people taste mercy, they rejoice in it; but if an evil befalls them because of what their hands have sent forth, behold, they despair.﴾

It is fine that people rejoice and rejoice in the mercy of God, but what is wrong with them that when an evil befalls them because of what their hands have sent forth, they despair? The course of mercy is the course of evil, but they rejoiced in the first because it is beneficial in their view, and despaired in the other because it is not beneficial in their view. They should have known that this and that are from God, and that He, glorified is He, has wisdom in mercy and wisdom in calamity also.

So: you looked at one thing and neglected another. You looked at what came about of mercy and what came about of calamity, and you did not look at Who brought about the mercy and Who brought about the calamity. If you had linked the existence of mercy or calamity to the One who did it, you would have known that He is Wise in this and in that. The affliction of people is that they separate the decrees from the One who decrees them. So you should not look at the reality itself, but at the One who brought this reality about.

Consider: your child comes to you crying because someone hit him. The first thing you rush to ask is: who did this to you? If he says: so-and-so, you say: yes, he hates us and wants to harm us... etc. If he says: my uncle hit me, you say: you must have done something that angered him, or you erred in something and he punished you for it.

So you did not look at the reality in itself; you linked it to the one who brought it about. If it came from the enemy, then he must intend evil; and if it came from the beloved, then he must intend good for you.

Likewise we should link what exists with the One who brought it into existence. If the One who brought the reality about is the Lord, then you must reflect on the wisdom. We will not speak of mercy, because its benefit is apparent to everyone; rather, let us ask about the calamity that grieves people, so that they despair and lose hope because of it.

We say: if you looked at the One who sent it upon you, your mind would be at ease and your soul would be reassured. Calamity means the thing that befalls you, whether good or bad. Do you not see His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from God, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself...﴾ (al-Nisa, 79)

Calamity is not blamed in itself; rather, the outcome of it is what matters. The word "asaba" (befall) used both for good and for evil indicates that its arrow has been shot at you, and its lifespan is the measure of its reaching you. It will surely strike you; it will not fail you or miss you, because the One who shot it is a God and a Wise Lord. If it is good, it will come to you, so do not weary yourself or crowd people over it; and if it is a calamity, beware of saying: I will guard against it to ward it off from myself, for there is no escape for you from it.

Then why do you despair and lose hope if a calamity befalls you? Why do you not wait and reflect? Perhaps it has a wisdom, and perhaps behind it is a good you do not know now; and perhaps the hardship will soon be followed by relief.

Have you not read: ﴿It may be that you dislike a thing and it is good for you; and it may be that you love a thing and it is bad for you...﴾ (al-Baqara, 216)

Do you remember the incident of the "Death Building," from which they expelled the doorkeeper and his family, and made it a court case; and after the building collapsed, it became clear to the doorkeeper and his family that what they had thought to be evil and calamity was in fact pure good.

So: do not despair over a harm that has befallen you; know that the One who caused it to happen to you is your Lord, and that He has a wisdom in it. Wait until it is revealed to you. Only one who has no Lord to turn to despairs.

Then let us discuss the calamity over which you despaired: do you have a part in it, or not? If you have a part in it, like the student who neglected his lessons and failed the exam, then you must receive this calamity with contentment, for the failure corrects your error and draws your attention to the negligence on your part, so that you may remedy the matter and strive.

But if the calamity has no part of yours in it, like one who studied and exerted himself, yet was not granted success due to an illness that struck him on the night of the exam, or some obstacle that came upon him, we say: beware of separating the calamity from its course and its Doer. Rather, reflect on the good that follows it, and do not separate the calamity from its course upon you, and do not despair.

Seek the wisdom of your Lord in sending this calamity upon you, like the mother who says to her son: "My son, you are always outstanding, and people envy you for your excellence; perhaps your failure will divert their envy from you, save you from their eyes, and they will leave you alone."

And when his father comes and says to him: "My son, take it easy; perhaps if you succeed this year you will not obtain the total you want, and this is an opportunity for you to strengthen yourself and obtain a higher total." So: you will not lack benefit behind the calamity, for your Lord is Self-Subsisting (al-Qayyum), who wills for you nothing but good.

Therefore, when you survey events you find people who were disgraced and taken to account for what they did not do, and who became victims of a false witness or a judge who ruled by whim... etc. But because your Lord is Self-Subsisting, who does not neglect, He compensates this wronged person and says to him: "A point has become yours with Me in your account. You were accused unjustly, so if you commit a crime I will save you from it, so that you are not punished for it. And you, O you who blinded yourself to justice, bore false witness, or took what was not yours, or escaped punishment: I will surely bring you into a crime you did not commit."

So: despair at the moment of calamity has no place. Had you linked the calamity to its Doer, you would have known that He is Wise, and that there must be a wisdom which may be hidden from you now, but when you turn the matter over in your mind, you will arrive at this wisdom.

When we look at the style of the verse, we find many contrasts. In speaking of mercy, He said ﴿And when We let people taste mercy, they rejoice in it...﴾ (al-Rum, 36), using the conditional particle "idha" (when).

As for calamity, He said ﴿But if an evil befalls them because of what their hands have sent forth, behold, they despair﴾ (al-Rum, 36), using the conditional particle "in" (if). Why did He depart from the monotony of the style, from "idha" to "in"?

They said: when you compare the blessings with the calamities that befall a person in his life, you find that the blessings are many and the calamities few. The blessings of God follow upon you at every time, countless and uncountable, while calamities can perhaps be counted on the fingers.

Therefore, with blessings He used "idha", which indicates certainty, and with calamity He used "in", which indicates doubt. Of the same kind is His saying: ﴿When the help of God and the victory come﴾ (al-Nasr, 1), where He used "idha" because it indicates certainty and makes the occurrence of victory likely; and He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And if any of the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection...﴾ (al-Tawba, 6).

We also notice in the style of the verse that it did not mention the cause for the tasting of mercy, but mentioned the cause of the calamity: ﴿because of what their hands have sent forth...﴾ (al-Rum, 36), to show His justice in sending calamity and His bounty in granting mercy, for mercy is from God and blessings are a bounty from God.

But regarding calamity He said ﴿because of what their hands have sent forth...﴾ (al-Rum, 36), mentioning the cause, so that no one thinks that God sends calamity upon His servant unjustly; rather, it is because of what his own hands have sent forth. The matter is governed by Divine justice.

Between bounty and justice there is a vast difference. If two litigants come to you for judgment, you say: "I will judge between you with justice, or with something better than justice?" They say: "Is there anything better than justice?" So: we want justice, but be mindful that justice gives you your right, while bounty leaves you your right(1) [sic].

It is as if the Truth, glorified is He, is saying to us: beware of thinking that you are saved by your deeds, no; rather by His bounty upon you: ﴿Say: "In the bounty of God and in His mercy—in that let them rejoice; it is better than what they accumulate."﴾ (Yunus, 58)

That is: however much of acts of obedience you accumulate, they will not suffice you, and there is no salvation for you except by mercy from God and bounty.

So the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, wants us to know that the mercy of God encompasses everything, and that, despite the blessings He has bestowed upon you, countless and uncountable, He will not punish you except for something you have committed that deserves punishment; because He is a Lord, Merciful and Wise.

Since this is the case, look at the effects of your Lord's mercy in the universe, reflect on these blessings, and pause at the precision of the style in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And if you tried to count the favours of God, you could not number them...﴾ (Ibrahim, 34)

Counting implies multiplicity, and "ni'ma" (favour) is singular in ﴿favours...﴾ (Ibrahim, 34). How then can we count, O Lord? They said: it is one favour, but within it are favours; if you examined it, you would find within it elements of goodness that cannot be counted or numbered.

Therefore, when the verses addressed the counting of God's favours, He used "in" (if), which indicates doubt, because they do not fall under limitation or counting; but even if you try to count them, you will not number them. Now, with the advance of the sciences and the specialization of entire faculties in the study of statistics, and their coming out to us with statistics on many matters and things in our lives, yet no one has attempted to count God's favour. Why?

Because turning to statistics is only done when there is an expectation that what is counted can be contained and encompassed by counting; but if it is beyond the range of your grasp, you will not attempt to compute it, just as no one has attempted, for example, to count the sand of the desert. Therefore God casts doubt upon you as to whether you could count them: ﴿And if you tried to count...﴾ (Ibrahim, 34), for it is a remote matter that will never happen.

1 "Watarahu haqqahu wa malahu": he diminished him his due and his property, i.e., reduced it for him. In the revealed Book: ﴿And He will not deprive you of your deeds﴾ (Muhammad, 35), meaning He will not diminish any of your reward. (Lisan al-Arab, root w-t-r). The intended meaning is that judgment by justice gives each of the litigants his right, whereas with bounty, the judge may look to the virtue of one of them, his high aspiration and nobility, and diminish his right, because he knows his sound intellect, contentment and chastity. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 30, verse 37:

"Yabsutu" (yabsut): He expands (yuwassi'). "Yaqdiru" (yaqdir): meaning He restricts (yudayyiq).

Meaning: Have you not seen this matter? One person has his provision expanded by God, and another has it restricted. Often the one of abundance has not toiled for it; it came to him from an inheritance or something else, while the one of restriction struggles and labours, yet his livelihood is merely sufficient. Therefore the philosophers have met this question with whatever is in their hearts of faith or atheism. Thus Ibn al-Rawandi (1), the atheist, says:

How many a learned man whose doctrines have baffled him, and how many an ignorant fool you meet enjoying provision!
This is the one who left the illusions bewildered, and made the brilliant scholar a heretic.

Another, from among those whose hearts were filled with faith, replied to him:

How many a learned man is in hardship, and how many an ignorant fool is in ease!
People were perplexed by this, so I said to them: this is what necessitates belief in predestination (al-qadar).

The world does not move by a fixed mechanical motion; rather, it moves by the self-subsistence (qayyumiyyah) of the Creator, glory be to Him, over it. So look at the expansion for whom God expands it, and the restriction for whom God restricts it, and do not detach the act from its Agent, glory be to Him. Reflect that God, the Exalted, is One, and that His servants are equal in His sight, yet He expands for one of them and restricts for another.

Therefore: there must be wisdom in this, and another wisdom in that. If you were to follow the consequences of expansion here and restriction there, the wisdom would appear to you.

Do you not see a man of abundance, of provision and many blessings, who nevertheless could not raise his children, because the manifestations of luxury swept them into deviation, and they failed in their practical lives? On the other hand, we see the poor man who lives on mere sufficiency, whose children excel and attain the highest ranks? Therefore: ﴿He expands the provision for whom He wills and restricts [it]...﴾ (al-Rum 37) according to a wisdom known to Him, glory be to Him and exalted.

We have previously mentioned that in Germany there are two philosophical schools of atheism, one belonging to a man named (Jabil), and the other to (Bakhtar). One of them denies that the world has a god, saying: "If the world had a wise god, He would not have created the blind, the lame, the one-eyed... etc. Wisdom in creation requires equality." He took the deviance in creation as evidence for his atheism.

As for the other, he said: "There is no god for the universe; it moves in a regular, mechanical course, and if there were a god in it, He would create creatures in varied forms, and He would have an absolute will free from mechanism." He took the stability of the order as evidence for his atheism, in order to contradict the doctrine of his predecessor.

Therefore: the matter for them is a desire for atheism by any means and in any form, and the use of a crooked method that serves the proposition they seek to establish.

Our reply to the first, who took deviance in the cosmos as evidence that there is no wise god, is: the deviance you mention is deviance in individuals, which some compensate for one another. One is blind, another one-eyed, and against them stand millions who see. The existence of this small proportion does not spoil the general rule of creation, nor does it affect the movement of humanity in the universe; the sound compensates for the unsound.

As for the fixed order that the second seeks, let him look at the higher realm (al-Mala' al-A'la) and the upper cosmos of sun, moon, stars... etc. He will see in it an order that does not change, for deviance in these creatures would corrupt the whole universe; therefore God created it upon stability and absence of deviance.

Therefore: in the general order of the cosmos we find stability, and in individuals, who are such that one of them can dispense with another, we find deviance and difference. Stability establishes the wisdom of power, and deviance establishes the freedom of power.

So, O you who want the stability of order as proof of faith: stability exists. And O you who want the deviance of order as proof of faith: deviance exists. There is nothing for you both but to agree, and for each of you to open himself to the other, so that you may reach the truth.

The matter of provision has a philosophy in Islam. The Truth, glory be to Him, has informed us that He is the Provider (al-Razzaq). Sometimes He provides through means, and sometimes He provides without means. But beware of being deceived by means: you may advance the means and strive, and then provision comes from them, or your striving fails, like the farmer who takes the means until the crop nearly reaches its full growth, then a calamity comes and destroys it. So beware of being deceived by means, and look to the Causer, glory be to Him.

We have said: one should seek out the means to provision, and then not preoccupy one's mind with its affair, for your Creator, who summoned you into existence, has undertaken it. The poet expressed this meaning in his saying:

Seek out its means to provision, and do not preoccupy yourself afterward with its concern.
For you do not know its address, while your provision knows your address.

Then He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe﴾ (al-Rum 37). He said "for a people who believe" because this matter of provision requires faith in the wisdom of the Provider, glory be to Him, in giving and in withholding.

We note in the verse's wording, the Exalted, regarding expansion: ﴿for whom He wills...﴾ (al-Rum 37), and regarding restriction: ﴿and restricts...﴾ (al-Rum 37), and He did not say "for whom" in the restriction. This is because expansion, in our view, is a thing loved, for which we rejoice and which we desire, so He said ﴿for whom He wills﴾ so that we may be reassured that we will be among those to whom provision is expanded. As for constriction, He did not say "for whom," so that it remains vague, which each of us dismisses from himself.

(1) He is: Ahmad ibn Yahya ibn Ishaq, Abu al-Husayn al-Rawandi, an openly declared atheist philosopher, from the residents of Baghdad, his nisba being to "Rawand," one of the villages of Isfahan. Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani said: He was at first one of the Mu'tazilite theologians, then he became a heretic and became famous for atheism. He composed a book on the eternity of the world, denied the Creator, corrected the doctrine of time (dahr), refuted the people of tawhid, and wrote a book attacking Muhammad (ﷺ). He died in the year 298 AH between al-Raqqa and Baghdad. (al-A'lam of al-Zirikli 1/267).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 30, verse 38:

Then the Lord of Glory, glorified is He, says:

﴿So give the near of kin his due, and the needy and the wayfarer. That is better for those who seek the Face of Allah, and it is they who are the successful.﴾ (30:38)

When we contemplate the Qur'anic arrangement here, we find that Allah, exalted is He, first mentioned the expansion of provision, then its restriction, and then immediately after it affirmed the right of the near of kin, the needy and the wayfarer. It is as if He is drawing our attention to the fact that these rights are not confined to those whose provision has been expanded; rather they are owed by everyone, even by one who is in want and whose provision has been constricted, so that he does not forget these people.

Therefore, Allah, glorified is He, concludes the verse with His saying: ﴿That is better for those who seek the Face of Allah, and it is they who are the successful.﴾ (30:38) And all of them, whether one whose provision has been expanded or one whose provision has been restricted, seek the Face of Allah.

When comparing this verse with the verse of zakat: ﴿The alms are only for the poor and the needy, and those employed to collect them, and those whose hearts are to be reconciled, and for freeing captives and debtors, and for the cause of Allah, and for the wayfarer; an obligation from Allah, and Allah is Knowing and Wise.﴾ (9:60)

Here the near of kin, mentioned in this verse, is not mentioned, and it is as if the verse points us to a matter that we should pay attention to: that giving one's relative from the wealth of zakat is a fault into which many of the rich, and even the religiously committed among them, have fallen. Often they ask: "I have a cousin, or a relative; should I give him something from my zakat money?"

I used to say to the questioner: "By Allah, does your cousin know that you are giving him from zakat money, and would he accept it from you? For the relative has a right, whether you are wealthy possessing the zakat threshold (nisab), or you have not reached the threshold."

So, do not link these three, the relative, the needy and the wayfarer, to the matter of zakat, for the right is owed even to the poor one who does not possess the nisab, and to the one whose provision is restricted.

Along with this right that the Sharia has established for the relative, we find many people consuming the rights of relatives and devising ways to deprive them of them. For example, some people do not have sons, so they write their property over to their daughters in order to deprive their paternal uncle or cousins of inheritance, although the daughter has half the estate, and if there are more than one, they have two-thirds, and the remaining third is distributed to the uncle or the cousin; this is because in such a case the daughters have no male agnatic heir (ʿasabah), so the Sharia assigns it to the uncle or the cousin.

The Wise Lawgiver balances the parties: He takes from you and gives to you. So why, when the father dies leaving these daughters, who have no inheritance, and who will depend on the uncle or cousin for support and bring him to court, do we deprive them of their rights and demand our own rights? This is a kind of foolishness.

Why do we not give the uncle or the cousin, who is the one who will protect the daughters, watch over their comfort, and stand beside them in their hardship?

So beware, then, of bringing relatives into zakat, or of linking their assistance to ability; for they have a right over you in your ease and in your hardship.

It is sufficient that Allah, exalted is He, singled them out with His saying: ﴿the near of kin...﴾ (30:38), and did not say: "the one in need" or "the wayfarer." The word (dhu), meaning "possessor of," indicates constant companionship and attachment. We do not say "So-and-so is a possessor of knowledge" of one who knows a matter or two; rather it is said of one who is characterized by wide knowledge and has mastered it. Likewise we do not say "So-and-so is a possessor of character" unless character is an attribute that is constant in him and never leaves him.

From this, we say: "dhu al-qurba" means one who is adjacent to you and does not leave you; therefore his right upon you must be observed, so you must give him a share, even if you do not possess the nisab. Likewise for the needy and the wayfarer, because Allah mentioned them together outside the category of zakat, which indicates that they have a right apart from the obligatory zakat.

We notice that the Qur'an arranged them according to importance and need: first the near of kin, because of his established kinship with you; then the needy, who is a known resident of your locality; then the wayfarer, the passerby whom you see one day and do not see afterwards. Each is according to his position in circumstance.

The needy's condition may change, and provision may become easy for him, and Allah may expand upon you; and the wayfarer returns to his own country. So the permanent description belongs to the near of kin; therefore Allah described him with what indicates permanence.

Then He said: ﴿its due...﴾ (30:38). The right is attached to him and he has the greater claim to it. Therefore He did not say, for example: "And give the near of kin his due, and the needy and the wayfarer their dues."

They have illustrated this by saying: "The commander said: Let so-and-so, and so-and-so, and so-and-so enter," and the permission to enter given to the first is followed by the rest.

So these three have a particularity: Allah has commanded you to give them of your flesh (i.e., your own substance), and not to link them to zakat, and to not withhold provision from them. As for the remaining seven who are entitled to zakat, you are not obliged toward them with anything beyond the obligatory zakat.

When a debate arose among the scholars concerning what is meant by the needy (miskin) and the poor (faqir), which of them is more in need than the other? They said: the miskin is one who has property but it does not suffice him. Abu Hanifa cited in support of this meaning the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿As for the boat, it belonged to needy men who worked on the sea...﴾ (18:79), where He established ownership for them and called them needy (masakin). As for the faqir, he is one who has nothing; on this basis the faqir is more in need than the miskin, and he is included in this verse a fortiori.

As for His saying: ﴿That...﴾ (30:38), i.e., giving to these, ﴿is better...﴾ (30:38). The word khayr is used in the language with one of two meanings: sometimes we say khayr, and its opposite is sharr, as in His saying: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it. And whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ (99:7-8); and sometimes we say khayr and mean "the better," i.e., the comparative form, as in the saying of the poet:

Zayd is the best of people, and the son of the best.

But what is common is that khayr is used in the comparative sense, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The strong believer is better and more beloved to Allah than the weak believer, and there is good in each." So the first khayr means "better." But for whom?

﴿For those who seek the Face of Allah...﴾ (30:38), i.e., in fulfilling the right of the near of kin, the needy and the wayfarer, they intend thereby the Face of Allah, not showing off or seeking reputation; for one who does good takes his reward from the one for whose sake he did it. So whoever works for Allah sincerely, his reward is with Allah, and whoever works for people out of showing off and seeking reputation, let him take his reward from them.

As for those whom Allah described with His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain, which the thirsty one thinks is water, until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing, and finds Allah with him, and He pays him his account in full. And Allah is swift in account﴾ (24:39), i.e., he is surprised to find a God whom he had not had in mind and for whom he had not worked.

So the meaning of ﴿seek the Face of Allah...﴾ (30:38) is that they intend by their deeds the Face of Allah, whether people see it or he conceals his deed, until "his left hand does not know what his right hand has done," because the matter rests on intention. You may give in front of people while your intention is that they follow your example, or to silence their tongues and their slander against you.

When you give openly with a sincere intention for Allah, it is charity that multiplies the giving and multiplies the reward; therefore it will be an example to others so that they give, and you will have a reward like theirs, for whoever establishes a good practice has its reward and the reward of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection.

The Noble Qur'an presented this matter to us in His saying: ﴿O you who believe, do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury, like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day...﴾ (2:264)

Then He gives us an illustrative example: ﴿So his example is like that of a smooth rock with dust on it; a heavy rain strikes it and leaves it bare. They have no power over anything of what they have earned. And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾ (2:264)

The example of the one who shows off is like this smooth, slippery stone which, when rain strikes it, and it has a layer of dust upon it, the rain removes it, and it remains bare and smooth, retaining nothing and nothing grows on it.

This example embodies for us the failure of the striver who shows off, that he is a fool: he strove and exerted himself, and people benefited from his effort, his good extended to others, and he himself came out empty-handed of good and of reward.

Then Allah, glorified is He, mentions the opposite: ﴿And the example of those who spend their wealth seeking the approval of Allah and for the strengthening of their souls is like a garden on a height; a heavy rain strikes it, and it produces its fruit twofold. And if no heavy rain strikes it, then a light rain. And Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾ (2:265)

So charity given seeking the Face of Allah is like fertile land upon which rain descends, so its vegetation comes forth multiplied and blessed. If there is no rain, the dew suffices it so that it grows and bears its fruit. Had He said "like a garden" it would have sufficed, but He said ﴿a garden on a height﴾ (2:265), i.e., on an elevated place, to indicate its fertility; for whenever the land is elevated its fertility increases, and it is free of groundwater that affects vegetation.

This garden is watered by rain that comes to it from above, which washes the leaves and branches, so their freshness and quality increase, and leaves are the lungs of the plant.

Allah, exalted is He, leaves in the traces of the self among people a reminder and a lesson. One person does good to another in order to buy him with it, or to subdue his neck through this favour; so the natural result is that the other denies his favour, and even hates him and bears a grudge against him. This is a fitting recompense for one who does a deed for other than the Face of Allah.

This is the meaning of their saying: "Beware the evil of the one to whom you have done good." Why? Because when he sees you he recalls your hand upon him and your favour, so he is humiliated and feels abased; for your presence crushes his pride, so he hates your presence and dislikes seeing you.

Allah, glorified is He, says: Beware of nullifying kindness by showing off, or by base motives; for this kindness of yours will be denied, and what you have done of good will be turned into evil against you. So, then: direct your deeds to the Face of Allah, not to anything else; if your favour is denied, your reward is preserved with Allah, and it is as if your Lord, mighty and majestic, is jealous over you, wanting to preserve your favour for you and store it with Him.

This meaning was expressed by the poet in his saying:

I say to the people of noble character a saying that comforts them if they do good and bestow favour:
The needy walk behind you humbly; if they reach it, they follow you and hasten.
So do not abandon kindness, however they deny it, for the reward of Allah is greater and more abundant.

I had previously mentioned the story of the man who met us on the road when we were in Algeria: he signaled to us to take him in our direction, so the car's owner stopped and opened the door for him, but before he got in he said, "How much?" meaning the price of his ride. The car's owner said, "For Allah." The man said, "Make it a good price, sheikh."

Therefore some of the knowers say: those who seek by their deeds the Face of Allah are those who raise the value of their deeds, that is, they increase their worth and multiply their reward.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So give the near of kin his due, and the needy and the wayfarer...﴾ (30:38), after His saying: ﴿and restricts...﴾ (30:37), indicates on its apparent sense that He takes from you even though you are poor; this falls within the scope of His saying: ﴿and they prefer [others] over themselves, even though they themselves are in need﴾ (59:9).

We have said that the Lawgiver is Wise; so when He obliges you and takes from you, it is only that He may give to you if you are in need. It is as if He says to you: Be at ease, for I have secured your life for you; if poverty befalls you, or one day you become needy or a wayfarer, then as you have done, so will be done to you.

This matter is clear in the sponsorship of the orphan. Were the believing community to compensate him for his father, in accordance with the Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "I and the one who sponsors an orphan are like these two in Paradise," (he gestured with his index and middle fingers), every father would be reassured about his children should he die and leave them, because they would be in a society that compensates them for their father with many fathers.

A person, if he is secure and blessed, is troubled in this blessing only by the fact that it is liable to vanish. So Allah wishes to secure for His servant a dignified life extending beyond him. This is the true insurance which Allah has set up as an insurance matter in the universe, not in insurance companies, but in His hand, glorified is He, where He said:

﴿And let those fear who, if they left behind them weak offspring, would be anxious for them. So let them fear Allah and speak words of appropriate justice.﴾ (4:9) When they fear Allah and speak the right word, their orphan will meet people who will sponsor him, be concerned for him, and take charge of his affairs.

We previously discussed, in Surat al-Kahf, the story of the wall which al-Khadir (peace be upon him) volunteered to build, although it was in a village whose people were miserly, who refused them even food. We said: asking for food is the most honest request, and its asker should not be turned away.

1 al-Gharimun: plural of gharim. A gharim is one upon whom a debt has been imposed, rightfully or wrongfully. And al-maghram: the fine, and a heavy debt. (al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/52).

2 From Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The needy one is not the one who goes around among people, so that a morsel or two morsels, a date or two dates are returned to him." They said: "Then who is the needy one, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "The one who does not find sufficient wealth to suffice him, and is not noticed so that he may be given charity, and does not ask people for anything." Narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (4539) and Muslim in his Sahih (1039), Kitab al-Zakat; the wording is Muslim's.

3 Narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad (2/366-370), Muslim in his Sahih (2664), and Ibn Majah in his Sunan (79), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him).

4 al-Safwan: a large hard rock that is smooth and produces nothing. (Lisan al-Arab, root ṣ-f-w). al-Ṣaldu: the smooth one unfit for planting. al-Wabil: heavy rain. (al-Qamus al-Qawim lil-Qur'an al-Karim).

5 From the poetry of the Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him.

6 Narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (6005) from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd, and by Muslim in his Sahih (2983) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him). The complete hadith: "and he said with his two fingers, the index and the middle finger." The meaning of al-sabbabah: because with it one points at the devil then. In another narration "al-sibahah," because with it one glorifies (yusabbih) in prayer, and so it is pointed with in the tashahhud. Said by Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani in Fath al-Bari (10/436).

7 al-Lu'am: plural of la'im, one who is base in origin and miserly of soul. (Lisan al-Arab, root l-´-m).

Then the Truth, glorified is He, tells us about the distinction between a gift (hibah) and charity (sadaqah), saying:

﴿And whatever you give in riba [to increase] within the wealth of people will not increase in the sight of Allah. But what you give in zakah, desiring the Face of Allah – those are the ones who receive multiplied [reward].﴾ (30:39) [riba: excess, increase (i.e., the gift given in expectation of a greater return)]

The Truth, glorified and exalted is He, knows that His creatures do good and seek reward for it, but this seeking may be lost if they show off in their deeds. The reward is proportionate to the deed if it is free from showing off. However, Allah, glorified is He, wants to raise charity or zakah to a high level, so the one who gives it receives its reward from the Hand of Allah, glorified is He, multiplied. Seeking increases lies in the intention.

For example, the believer knows that if he is greeted with a greeting, he must return it with something better. A poor man may present a gift to one of the wealthy according to his ability, and in his intention is that the rich man return it in a manner suited to his wealth. Thus, when he gives, he hopes for increase, even though it is not stipulated. The rich man may return the gift with something better, or he may not return it at all.

So His saying, ﴿And whatever you give in riba...﴾ (30:39), means: the increase in any of its forms over what you give. This increase is not stipulated in a contract, and the increase may be in wealth or by any other means that carries benefit, because they defined riba as: every loan that draws a benefit is riba.(2)

Indeed, Imam Abu Hanifah used to sit in the shade of a wall belonging to his neighbour. When he asked his neighbour for money and borrowed it, the neighbour saw that he no longer sat in the shade of the wall as he used to. He asked him about that, and he said: "I used to sit in the shade of your wall, knowing that it was a favour from you. Now I fear that I would sit there lest you think this sitting is for the money you took from me."

So the meaning is: whatever riba you give, seeking increase by it, whether it be benefit, or wealth, or something other than wealth, whether stipulated or not stipulated. They said: What is the ruling on gifts if they are returned with something better? And what is my fault, I who gave? They said: There is nothing wrong in it, provided that you do not intend increase in it, and that your gift is not stipulated; rather, it is a means of affection, goodwill and kindness among people, but you do not take a reward for it from Allah.

His saying ﴿ليربو في أموال الناس﴾ [that it may increase within the wealth of people] – here "في" is for location (zarfiyyah): wealth is a vessel, and what you put into it diminishes from it and increases what you have. ﴿فلا يربو عند الله﴾ [it does not increase in the sight of Allah] – it increases for you yourself through the increase you take from the one you greeted, but in the sight of Allah it does not increase.

Thus said Ibn 'Abbas(3), although some scholars said: it is general concerning riba in its original sense; this is a matter that should be given attention, but Ibn 'Abbas saw that the verse on riba is well known, and this verse is about riba in the increases of greetings and courtesies among people.

Then He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And whatever you give in zakah, desiring the Face of Allah – those are the ones who receive multiplied [reward].﴾ (30:39) That is: those who give zakah and intend thereby the Face of Allah. ﴿هم المضعفون﴾ [those are the ones who receive multiplied (reward)] – it is not from *idhaf* (doubling as a transgression of the lender), but from *adh‘aaf* (multiplication of reward); zakah is *adh‘af* with a fatḥah (أضعاف), as in His saying: ﴿Who is it that would lend to Allah a goodly loan so He will multiply it for him...﴾ (57:11). As for riba, it is *idhaf* with a kasrah.

Some orientalists who like to find fault with the words of Allah have paused at this matter. They said: "There are verses in the Qur'an that contradict the Prophetic hadith. The Qur'an says: ﴿Who is it that would lend to Allah a goodly loan so He will multiply it for him...﴾ (57:11)."

So: a goodly loan is multiplied by Allah in reward, and you hold that a good deed is multiplied tenfold. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is written on the gate of Paradise: the good deed is rewarded tenfold, and the loan with eighteen." If a goodly loan multiplies the good deed tenfold, then it is twenty, not eighteen.

We said to him: If you gave a dollar in charity, for example, you have done a good deed which is multiplied up to ten. But do I return to you the dollar you gave in charity? No. So the reality is that you received nine multiplied to eighteen.

They said: Why then is the reward of a loan greater? We say: Because the one who gives charity, when he gives it, his hope in what he has sent forward is cut off; but the lender remains preoccupied with the loan, awaiting its repayment, so whenever he is patient with it he receives reward. Moreover, the borrower borrows only out of need, whereas the one who receives charity may accept it while not needing it, and perhaps he is one of those who hoard wealth.

So: the Truth, glorified is He, wants to make the loan grow. Why? They said: Because Allah wants the movement of life to proceed and to be complete. You take pride in your wealth, fear for it, and want it to grow, and you will find all of this in the loan. So make it a loan; it is the door that Allah has opened for you for increase and reward.

Then Allah, exalted is He, has respected your ownership of your wealth and was keen to protect it for you, so He says: ﴿O you who have believed, when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down...﴾ (2:282)

Allah safeguards your wealth for you so that you may be at ease about it, and yet He leaves room for the generosity and nobility of the giver: ﴿And if one of you entrusts another, let the one who is entrusted fulfil his trust and fear Allah, his Lord...﴾ (2:283)

By this faithful philosophy wealth circulates and the movement of life proceeds, such that the owner of wealth is guaranteed his wealth, because he loves it and is keen upon it, and the one who has no wealth is guaranteed the ability to move with the wealth of others. If there is a trust to be discharged, then every holder of a trust must discharge it to its rightful owner.

But if these balances are disturbed, and the poor man delays repayment to the rich man and is niggardly about returning his right, then the condition of society has become corrupt and these values have collapsed. At that point we cannot blame the one able to give if he withholds his wealth from those in need of a loan – and why not, when people are devouring rights? Thereby the movement of life stops and society falls back from keeping pace with the movement of progress.

So if the riba that is not stipulated – which is riba in gifts, courtesies and greetings among people – Allah made it a matter of nobility among people, for which He neither rewards nor punishes, and He said of it: ﴿it does not increase in the sight of Allah...﴾ (30:39)

As for stipulated riba, He took a firm stand against it, prescribed a punishment for it, and made this punishment of a kind that opposes the aim of the one who practises riba. You practise riba to increase your wealth, and Allah meets you with diminution: ﴿Allah destroys riba...﴾ (2:276). Why?

They said: Because the giver is wealthy and has, a surplus of wealth from which he gives, whereas the taker is in need. How can we demand of the one in need that he increase the wealth of the wealthy one who is not in need? And how will the needy person regard you when he knows that you have wealth beyond your need, and yet you refuse to lend him a goodly loan, but instead stipulate an increase upon him, taking the increase from him while he is in need?

Then suppose I took this loan to invest and grow it, and I lost. Is it not enough that I lose my work and my effort is wasted? Is it just that I lose my work and then also be guarantor of the increase? This is not justice, because the condition of a contract is that it protect the interest of both parties, whereas a riba contract protects only the interest of the creditor.

We see that even man-made economic legislation, when a bank gives money to a person for a project, for example, and he loses, and they wish to settle his situation, the first thing in their procedures is to waive the interest from him.

This agrees with the law of Allah in His saying: ﴿And if you repent, you will have your capital; you will not wrong, nor will you be wronged.﴾ (2:279) ("you will not wrong" means: we return your capital to you; "nor will you be wronged" means: we do not wrong you from another direction, so we say to you:

If you wish to repent, return what you took by riba with retroactive effect, because what you took has been spent and it is difficult to restore it. In this way we observe the interest of the creditor when we return the principal to him, and the interest of the debtor, so we do not burden him with returning what he cannot return.

When we reflect on this matter: which are stronger, states or individuals? States. Have you seen a state that borrowed money from another state and was able to pay the interest on that debt, let alone the principal? Likewise, strong individuals who take loans and then cannot even pay the interest, nor can they reschedule it or settle their situation, and so they fall into disputes and problems.

Another point: suppose a man has, for example, a thousand pounds, and another man has nothing. The owner of the thousand can manage it and live off it, whereas the other who owns nothing borrows in order to live like his companion. If you say to him: "The thousand as a loan for a hundred pounds," from where will he find this hundred?

If he takes it from the return on the capital, he loses; if he takes it from the commodity, by reducing its quality or its effective ingredients, or in its packaging, the commodity comes out inferior to its counterparts and fails to sell. So the consumer must bear it, and this is harm to him, though he is not a party to the contract. Thus the contract is void.

When we say that Islam is suitable for every time and place, we must understand this matter well, and beware of saying that Islam is not suitable in such-and-such a time or such-and-such a place.

Now we hear some turn away from the method of Islam and say to you: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity...﴾ (2:286) – meaning: it is not within its capacity now to implement the law of Allah. But we say to him: who determines the capacity? You, or the Lawgiver, glorified is He?

Since Allah has imposed the obligation, know that the obligation is within your capacity. Take capacity from the obligation; do not determine the capacity yourself and forget what Allah has obligated you with. Therefore you see that when capacity is constrained, Allah lightens it for you without your asking for leniency, as in the prayer and fasting of the sick and the traveller… etc., and as in tayammum when the use of water is impossible.

So there is no sense in saying: the teachings of religion do not suit the age. Then make the age the lawgiver, and turn away from the legislation of heaven to what the age can bear.

Therefore we have said: when the Truth, glorified is He, lays down His obligations, He says: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite...﴾ (6:151). The meaning of "come" (taʿālaw) is: rise above the level of human desires and ascend to the obligations of Allah. If you bring the obligations down to your own level and say, "the circumstances of the age compel me to do such-and-such," you have subjected the logic of heaven to the logic of earth, whereas the logic of heaven came only to elevate you.
